gloss: fold a whole shift into one “from X to Y” sentence
form: from X to Y; not X but Y
use: summarising a historical or conceptual change
example: “From deconstructing essences logically to showing how to stop imputing them psychologically.”
source: Waldron, Making Sense of Mind Only (prologue/intro sample)

gloss: change the question’s grammar or aspect to change what can be asked
form: ‘what is X?’ → ‘how does X come about?’; noun → verb
use: a question keeps producing essences
example: “The neuron is better understood as a verb than a noun.”

gloss: name a recurring tension once, then reuse the name
form: “what we will call the ___”
use: a problem keeps returning in different guises
example: “What we will call the Abhidharma Problematic.”

gloss: move a line instead of denying it exists
form: the line runs not between A and B, but between C and D
use: a dichotomy is felt but drawn in the wrong place
example: The private/shared line runs “not between our skin-encapsulated body and the world, but between our material senses and our ‘minds’.”

gloss: give a technical term its meaning, and its original, in passing
form: term (original): short gloss
use: introducing a term without stopping the sentence
example: “Each dharma was defined in terms of its own-being (svabhāva).”

gloss: divide a loaded term into its strong and weak senses before arguing
form: X in the strong sense vs. X in the weak sense
use: an argument trades on one word
example: “Depend upon mind”: a strong ontological dependence vs. a weaker epistemological one.

gloss: say what kind of claim it is before weighing it
form: this is a metaphor / remedy / definition, not an explanation / assertion
use: a sentence is being judged by the wrong standard
example: The seed “is a metaphor (not a dharma)”; Milinda’s similes “do not explain” continuity.

gloss: unpack a word’s parts when they carry the claim
form: split at the morpheme: in-dependent, de-sign-ate, vi-jñāna
use: the word’s structure already says the point
example: vi- ‘division’ in vijñāna: awareness arises by contrast, like noticing the fridge hum only when it stops.

gloss: set two contrasting axes to place things precisely
form: synchronic / diachronic; basis / object of analysis
use: a question mixes two dimensions
example: The ālaya analysed synchronically (what it supports now) and diachronically (what it carries over time).
checked: C1+C2; corrected (C2: old example read as contrastive compression)

gloss: sort a doctrine’s aims with a set of matched adverbs
form: thinking Xly, Yly, Zly
use: one teaching serves several purposes at once
example: The Buddha was thinking remedially, causally, soteriologically.

gloss: set a modern finding beside the classical text
form: classical claim + modern field’s parallel
use: showing an old idea is not merely old
example: Vasubandhu’s fused atoms beside the binding problem; afflicted mind beside the rubber-hand illusion.

gloss: set two hypotheses against what each would predict
form: if H1, expect E; if H2, expect not-E
use: two explanations both sound right
example: If composed in Chinese, the Sanskrit should show calques from Chinese; if in Sanskrit, the reverse.

gloss: state how sure you are, explicitly
form: Highly speculative: … / Confident: …
use: a bold claim sits beside solid ones
example: “Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need.”

gloss: expose an explanation that fits every outcome and so predicts nothing
form: its only evidence is that something is unexplained
use: a theory can never lose
example: “Superposition’s only symptom is that something doesn’t make sense.”

gloss: show a view was made the default when it should have been the last resort
form: X was the null hypothesis when it should have been the last
use: a field’s starting assumption went unexamined
example: “Making superposition the null hypothesis when it should have been the last hypothesis.”

gloss: show a method undercuts the aim it was built for
form: method M, pursued fully, defeats aim A
use: a system works against its own purpose
example: Momentariness would make afflictions ‘unreal’ — undercutting a path built to remove them.

gloss: apply your critique to your own method
form: our own X is also a case of what we criticise
use: you’re exempting your own frame
example: Modern historicism is itself just another doxographic rubric.
checked: C1+C2; corrected (C2: other half was a peritrope)

gloss: state a changed view plainly, and why the old one appealed
form: I used to think X; now Y; X felt right because Z
use: correcting yourself or your field
example: “Convinced much of the field, including me”; “superposition just felt right.”

gloss: an everyday image whose logic maps the problem exactly
form: the problem behaves like (everyday thing)
use: an abstract dilemma needs a picture
example: Self-grasping that vanished and returned would be like trick birthday candles that relight.

gloss: test a claim on its most extreme instance
form: picture P at its limit: (extreme case)
use: the stakes of a view are hidden
example: Without continuity, “Mother Theresa [sic] and Hitler would be in the same state right after they died.”
checked: C1+C2; corrected (C2: form read as reductio; C1: spelling as printed)

gloss: a precise two-word verdict
form: adjective + noun that delivers judgement
use: closing a point without a paragraph
example: “Explanatorily vacuous”; “a conceptual cul-de-sac.”

gloss: end with a few words that carry the whole argument
form: ‘Same ___, better ___.’
use: a long argument needs a handle to remember it
example: The last line of a long essay: “Same neurons, better microscope.”

gloss: a pun that carries the argument, not just decorates it
form: word A → related word B, where the link is the claim
use: only when the sound-link is the logical link
example: Habits of body, speech and mind give rise to “the habitats we inhabit.”

gloss: prefer the explanation with the fewest assumptions
use: two explanations fit the facts
example: The style dropped: a conditional trigger explains it without positing a memory leak.

gloss: a patient can have as many diseases as they please; the counterweight to Occam
use: one neat cause is tempting but the facts are many
example: Fatigue and back pain may be two problems, not one syndrome.

gloss: think of common causes before rare ones
use: a rare cause is exciting but unlikely
example: A headache after a short night: think sleep, not a tumour.

gloss: test first for the most likely cause (“go where the money is”)
use: choosing what to check first
example: A bug report? Check yesterday’s edited line before auditing the whole script.
checked: C1+C2; corrected (C2: too close to zebras)

gloss: don’t attribute to malice what stupidity explains
use: a slight feels deliberate
example: Housing answered half your email: assume overload, not dismissal.

gloss: what is asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence
use: a claim arrives with no support
example: “Research shows flashcards don’t transfer” — which study?

gloss: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence
use: a claim is far beyond the usual
example: A repo “reverse-engineers any firmware”: believe it after independent benchmarks, not its README.

gloss: no “ought” follows from an “is” alone
use: a fact is used to settle a duty
example: “Humans evolved to eat meat, so we ought to.”
checked: C1+C2; corrected (C2: gave the answer away)

gloss: refuting nonsense takes far more effort than producing it
use: deciding whether to answer a bad claim
example: One line — “meditation is just relaxation” — takes a whole lecture to unpack.
checked: C1+C2; corrected (C1: Nattier is the source of the thesis, not its rebuttal)

gloss: the harder reading is more likely original, because copyists simplify
use: two manuscript readings disagree
example: One witness has an awkward reading, another a smooth one: favour the awkward.

gloss: judging from only the cases that made it through a filter
use: your sample was pre-selected
example: Judging monastic life only by the monks who stayed.

gloss: searching where it’s easy to look, not where the answer is
use: the convenient source keeps getting used
example: Searching only what’s online when the reading is in an unscanned manuscript.

term: the map is not the territory
gloss: a model is not the thing it models (Korzybski)
use: a plan or theory is mistaken for the world
example: The timetable says 7:30 study; the morning says otherwise.

gloss: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
use: you are about to optimise a number
example: Aim at 200 Anki reviews a day and you start clicking “Good” on cards you half-know.
notes: popular wording usually credited to Marilyn Strathern

gloss: the more an indicator drives decisions, the more it is corrupted, and the more it distorts what it monitors
use: a metric starts deciding outcomes
example: When housing priority follows GPA, students start avoiding hard seminars.

gloss: a system mirrors the communication structure of the people who build it
use: a design’s seams look like an org chart
example: A booklet edited by three committees ends up in three styles.

gloss: a complex system that works grew from a simple one that worked; one designed from scratch never works
use: planning a big build from scratch
example: The meditation timer worked as “one bell, one knob” after the many-menu version failed.
checked: C1+C2; corrected (C1: example shows the second clause)

gloss: work expands to fill the time available
use: a task has no deadline
example: Given all Saturday for a two-hour task, it takes all Saturday.

gloss: people rise to the level of their incompetence
use: promotion rewards the old job, not the new one
example: The best translator, made editor, turns out a middling editor.

gloss: most effects come from a few causes (the 80/20 rule)
use: choosing what to fix or learn first
example: A small share of Pāli words makes up most of what you’ll read.

gloss: a fix that rewards the problem, and so grows it
use: an incentive could be gamed
example: Crediting whoever clears the biggest dish backlog — so people let the backlog pile up.
checked: C1+C2; corrected (C1+C2: must reward the problem)

gloss: the longer a non-perishable thing has lasted, the longer it’s likely to last
use: betting on what will endure
example: A 2,000-year-old sutta will likely outlast this year’s app.

gloss: don’t remove something until you know why it was put there
use: an old rule or rubric looks pointless
example: Don’t cut a line from the liturgy until you know why it’s there.

gloss: taking the first option that’s good enough (Herbert Simon)
use: searching for the best costs more than it gains
example: Buy the first warm Type B tube that fits and is in stock.

gloss: paralysis between two equally good options
use: two choices are close and time is passing
example: Two equally good winter retreats, and booking neither.

gloss: effort spent on the trivial part because it’s easy to argue about (Parkinson’s law of triviality)
use: a meeting is stuck on details
example: An hour on the cover font, ten minutes on the translation.

gloss: a chain of side tasks standing between you and the real one
use: you’re three steps removed from the goal
example: To print the cards, rebuild the script, which needs the font, which needs the repo…

gloss: it always takes longer than you expect, even allowing for Hofstadter’s law
use: estimating time
example: Budget double for the translation, and it still overruns the doubled budget.

gloss: won at a cost that defeats the purpose
use: a win would damage what you want
example: Winning the argument with Housing and losing their goodwill.

gloss: forcing material to fit a scheme
use: a framework is bending the facts
example: Forcing every weak argument into a named fallacy.

gloss: a consequence of a consequence
use: a change looks simple
example: Cheaper rides add traffic that slows every ride.

gloss: explaining a problem aloud exposes the error
use: you’re stuck
example: Spotting the bug halfway through describing it to Claude.

gloss: once noticed, a thing seems to appear everywhere
use: a new idea seems suddenly common
example: After learning “enthymeme”, hidden premises seem to be everywhere.

gloss: once you know something, it’s hard to imagine not knowing it
use: writing for beginners
example: A beginners’ Sanskrit handout that skips sandhi as obvious.

gloss: trusting a source on other topics after seeing it get your own field wrong (coined by Michael Crichton, 2002, after Murray Gell-Mann)
use: a source failed where you could check it
example: A paper botches Buddhism; you still trust its AI coverage.

gloss: advantage accrues to those who already have it (Robert Merton)
use: success seems self-reinforcing
example: Much-cited translators get cited more.

gloss: trying to suppress information spreads it
use: deciding whether to hide something
example: Banning a book in the dorm makes everyone read it.

gloss: the range of ideas acceptable in public discussion at a given time
use: an idea seems unsayable now
example: What a community can openly discuss shifts over decades.
